analysis.one_liner: Taxes businesses on the value of targeted state and local subsidies used to lure or keep them.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 1999 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: State and local governments compete with each other by offering tax breaks, cheap land, and other giveaways to individual companies to lure jobs across state lines. This bill would tax the value of those company-specific subsidies at the corporate rate, take away the tax exemption on bonds used to finance them, and bar federal money from being spent on them. Its stated goal was to end a bidding war that drains public budgets to benefit particular businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers in state and local governments that would no longer be pressured to outbid neighbors for companies, and businesses that compete on merit rather than negotiating subsidies. Ordinary residents keep tax dollars for schools, roads, and services that would otherwise go to individual companies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that state and local governments 'are being forced to compete against each other for businesses with scarce tax dollars that would otherwise be used for essential public goods and services,' and that no single government can unilaterally withdraw from this competition — only Congress can end it [S3].

It imposes an excise tax, computed at the corporate income tax rate, on the value of any benefit a business receives from a targeted subsidy — including tax abatements, below-market loans, free land or facilities, and loan guarantees [S3].

It denies federal tax exemption to interest on municipal bonds whose proceeds finance targeted development subsidies, removing a federal tax break that helps underwrite interstate bidding wars [S2],[S3].
It prohibits the use of federal grant funds for targeted subsidies and directs the Treasury Secretary to recover federal money spent in violation, with referral to the Attorney General [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that negotiate location or retention deals with state and local governments would pay tax on the value of those benefits, and bond investors and state economic development agencies would lose the tax-exempt financing tool. Local officials who use subsidies as an economic development strategy would lose a lever.

drawbacks.text: The definition of a targeted subsidy is broad: it covers not only explicit giveaways but any subsidy 'reasonably expected to have the effect' of encouraging a location decision, and even broadly available tax breaks that are not part of a government's 'general long-term' policy — so routine abatements and below-cost use of public facilities could be swept in, creating compliance burden and litigation [S3].

Subsidy competition can be a genuine tool for attracting jobs to areas with high unemployment; a blanket federal tax on those deals would take that option away from struggling cities and towns, and could push some companies to locate abroad instead [S3] (the bill itself acknowledges states use these deals to attract business, without a carve-out for distressed areas — its only exemption is for employee training and education [S3]).

Enforcement would require the Treasury to value each benefit — free roads, water, land — against a government's standard rates, an administratively complex undertaking that could produce uneven results across jurisdictions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea addresses a real, well-documented problem: governments spending scarce public money bidding against each other for companies that would often locate somewhere anyway, with the cost falling on ordinary taxpayers. The tax-on-value design is workable but blunt, and the sweeping definition could hit ordinary tax incentives, not just extravagant deals. On balance it is a serious attempt at a public-spirited reform, though a well-designed version would have needed clearer limits and perhaps relief for economically distressed areas.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. David Minge (D-MN) introduced the bill on March 10, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1],[S5].
Four members cosponsored it: three Democrats and one Independent [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee held no hearing or markup, and the full House never voted on it; the action history shows no step after the referral [S5].
The bill's own findings acknowledged that no single state can unilaterally stop competing for businesses and that only Congress has the power to end the bidding war [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that negotiate state and local subsidy packages, and the economic development agencies and bond-financing channels that support them, kept the status quo untouched. Taxpayers in competing jurisdictions continued footing the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Subsidy-receiving companies and state development agencies

for.name: Rep. David Minge
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed the problem: state and local governments bidding public dollars against each other for businesses, a race no single state can exit.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Bill Archer (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the four cosponsors were three Democrats and one Independent, so the record shows Democratic sponsorship but no way to measure broader party support or opposition.

industries.industry: Businesses receiving targeted state and local development subsidies
industries.note: The bill would tax the value of tax abatements, cheap land, below-market loans, and other location deals at the corporate rate, ending a major source of negotiated public money for individual companies. These companies profit from public budgets that ordinary taxpayers fund.

industries.industry: Municipal bond market / industrial development bond issuers
industries.note: Interest on bonds financing targeted development subsidies would lose its federal tax exemption, raising the cost of that financing and shrinking a tax-advantaged corner of the bond market.

industries.industry: State and local economic development agencies
industries.note: These agencies would lose their main tool — tax incentives and subsidized financing — for recruiting or retaining employers, which their staffs view as job creation but which the bill's findings describe as a wasteful interstate bidding war. The bill carves out subsidies for employee training and education.
